hero.title: Heights & Distances — Trigonometry You Can Actually Use
hero.hook: How do engineers measure the height of a mountain without climbing it? How did ancient astronomers calculate distances to stars? How do ships navigate without GPS? All of it uses one elegant idea — trigonometry applied to real triangles. And it's worth 4–6 marks in your board exam.

hook_section.scenario: You're standing 100m from the base of a building. You look up at the top — the angle between your line of sight and the ground is 45°. Without measuring the building directly, can you find its height? Yes — tan(45°) = height/100 → height = 100m. That's the entire chapter in one example.
hook_section.bridge: Heights and Distances is Chapter 9 in Class 10 Maths, and it always appears as a word problem in the exam. The trick is correctly identifying the angle of elevation or depression and setting up the right trigonometric ratio.
hook_section.punchline: Angle of elevation (looking up) and angle of depression (looking down) — master these two, and no problem can trip you.

concept_section.analogy: Every heights and distances problem is just a right triangle in disguise. You always know one angle and one side, and need to find another side. Your tools are three ratios: sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent. The choice depends on which sides are involved.
concept_section.principle: Key values: sin30°=½, cos30°=√3/2, tan30°=1/√3 | sin45°=1/√2, cos45°=1/√2, tan45°=1 | sin60°=√3/2, cos60°=½, tan60°=√3. Angle of elevation = angle above horizontal. Angle of depression = angle below horizontal.
concept_section.reveal_prompt: Tap each scenario to practise setting up the equation 👇

reveals.question: 🏢 Tower problem (single observer)?
reveals.answer: Observer at distance d, angle of elevation θ. Height h = d × tan θ. Draw the right triangle: observer at one corner, base of tower, top of tower.

reveals.question: 🌊 Two angles of elevation (same tower, two positions)?
reveals.answer: Observer moves closer — angle increases. Set up two equations with tan for both positions. Solve simultaneous equations for height and distance.

reveals.question: ✈️ Angle of depression from a height?
reveals.answer: Angle of depression from point A to point B = angle of elevation from B to A (alternate interior angles). Always redraw making these equal — most errors come from mixing them up.

reveals.question: 🗼 Two objects — finding distance between them?
reveals.answer: Often involves two towers or poles. Draw both right triangles sharing a common horizontal base. Set up equations for both heights, then find the gap between bases.

points: Angle of elevation: formed at observer's eye looking UP at an object above horizontal
Angle of depression: formed at observer's eye looking DOWN at an object below horizontal — equals angle of elevation from the lower object (alternate angles)
Always draw a diagram: label the right angle, angle given, side known, side needed
tan θ is used most often (involves height and base distance, not hypotenuse)
Standard angles 30°, 45°, 60° — memorise their exact trig values

exam_questions.question: A 10m tall building casts a shadow 10√3 m long. Find the angle of elevation of the sun
From the top of a 15m cliff, the angle of depression of a boat is 30°. Find the distance of boat from the base of cliff
The angle of elevation of a tower is 45° at a distance of 50m. What is the height of the tower?

quiz.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point 100m away is 30°. Height of tower is:
From the top of a building, angle of depression of a car is 45°. If building is 50m tall, distance of car from base is:
quiz.exp: Angle of depression = angle of elevation from car = 45°. tan45° = 50/d → d = 50m.

quiz.q: The angle of elevation of the sun when a pole 6m tall casts a shadow of 6m is:
quiz.exp: tan θ = height/shadow = 6/6 = 1. tan45° = 1, so θ = 45°.

quiz.q: Angle of depression and angle of elevation between two points are equal because:
quiz.exp: The horizontal from the observer and the ground are parallel lines cut by the line of sight. Angle of depression and angle of elevation are alternate interior angles — always equal.

flipcards.back: Angle formed at observer's eye when looking UP at an object — measured from horizontal

flipcards.front: If angle of depression is 30°, angle of elevation from below is?
flipcards.back: 30° — they are equal (alternate interior angles with parallel horizontal lines)

flipcards.front: Tower problem setup: observer 50m away, elevation 45°. Height?

flipcards.back: tan θ = opposite/adjacent — only uses height and base, no hypotenuse needed
